section.title: God Judges the Rulers
section.sectionRationale: A short, sharp Asaphite courtroom scene in which God takes His stand in the divine assembly and indicts human judges, called 'gods' because they exercise delegated authority, for failing to defend the weak. It closes with a plea for God Himself to judge the whole earth.
section.thesis: Every human authority holds delegated, borrowed power under God's own judgment, and true justice means defending the weak, the fatherless, and the oppressed, a standard only God's own righteous reign, previewed in this psalm and claimed by Jesus, can finally and fully satisfy.
section.frameNote: Five scenes: the Judge arrives, 1; the charges of unjust favoritism, 2-4; the diagnosis of moral blindness, 5; the verdict of mortality on unfaithful rulers, 6-7; and the closing appeal for God to judge the whole earth, 8.

units.label: The Judge arrives
units.note: God presides in the divine assembly

verses.text: God presides in the divine assembly; He renders judgment among the {{elohim|gods}}:
"How long will you {{shaphat|judge}} unjustly and show partiality to the wicked? Selah
Defend the cause of the weak and fatherless; uphold the rights of the afflicted and oppressed.
Rescue the weak and needy; save them from the hand of the wicked.
They do not know or understand; they wander in the darkness; all the foundations of the earth are shaken.

units.label: The verdict
units.note: sons of the Most High will die like mortals

verses.text: I have said, 'You are {{elohim|gods}}; you are all sons of the Most High.'
But like mortals you will die, and like rulers you will fall."

units.label: The appeal
units.note: arise, O God, judge the earth

verses.text: Arise, O God, judge the earth, for all the nations are Your inheritance.

elohim.gloss: God, or, applied to human judges, 'gods,' meaning those who exercise God-given authority to judge. The same word names both the LORD presiding, verse 1, and the corrupt human rulers He judges, verse 6, a wordplay Jesus cites in John 10:34 to defend His own claim to divine sonship.

shaphat.gloss: To judge, govern, or vindicate. God 'renders judgment' among the gods and commands them to 'judge' justly, verse 2, showing that all human judgment is meant to mirror His own righteous rule.

basic.context: In a vivid courtroom scene, God stands in the divine assembly and puts human judges, called 'gods' because they hold delegated authority, on trial for favoring the wicked and neglecting the weak, fatherless, afflicted, and oppressed. He pronounces that despite their exalted title, they will die like any mortal, and the psalm closes with a plea for God Himself to judge the whole earth.
basic.hermeneutics: The 'gods' here are not other deities but human judges or rulers, echoing Exodus 22:28's use of the same word for those who exercise judicial authority. The psalm indicts the abuse of real, God-given authority, not competing divine beings, and calls for God's own justice to prevail where human justice fails.
basic.originalLanguages: The word elohim names both the LORD who presides in judgment, verse 1, and the human authorities He judges, verse 6, since they exercise a derived, God-given office to shaphat, judge, on His behalf, an office they have corrupted through partiality.
basic.typology: The psalm's picture of God rising to judge the earth with perfect justice anticipates the final, universal judgment and reign of Christ, who alone judges without partiality and vindicates the oppressed completely.
basic.christ: Jesus quotes this psalm directly, John 10:34-36, arguing that if Scripture calls flawed human judges 'gods' because they bear a derived divine commission, it is no blasphemy for Him, sent and set apart by the Father, to call Himself God's Son.
basic.god: God is shown as the supreme Judge who holds every human authority accountable to His own standard of justice for the weak, and who will Himself rise to judge the earth perfectly and finally when human justice fails.
basic.crossReferences: John 10:34-36 shows Jesus using this psalm's language to defend His identity as the Son of God. Isaiah 3:13-15 pictures the LORD prosecuting leaders who crush His people, echoing this psalm's courtroom scene. Revelation 11:15 answers this psalm's closing plea, when the kingdoms of the world become the kingdom of the Lord.
basic.oneStory: This psalm's courtroom scene, exposing corrupt human authority and pleading for God's own righteous judgment over the earth, points forward to Christ, who both claims the divine authority this psalm implies and will one day judge the earth in perfect, final justice.

context.literary:
Psalm 82 is one of the shortest and sharpest scenes in the Psalter, and it is built as a single act of speech with a frame around it. Verse 1 is narration in the third person: God takes His stand and gives judgment. Verses 2 to 7 are God's own voice, beginning with a question, "How long," running through a string of commands in verses 3 and 4, pausing on a spoken aside in verse 5, and ending with a sentence that turns on one small word, "But," at the start of verse 7. Verse 8 is the worshipper's voice, the one line of plain prayer in the poem. The frame matters. A reader is first made a spectator of a trial, and only at the end is drawn into the courtroom as someone who has a stake in the outcome.

The psalm is also built on a hinge between two uses of one word. Elohim, the ordinary Hebrew word for God, stands in verse 1 for the Judge and for those He judges, and again in verses 6 and 8. The repetition is the argument. Everything the accused are called in verse 6 they have borrowed, and the first and last lines of the psalm remind them who owns the title. The middle of the sentence in verses 2 to 4 is worth noticing as well: four verbs of defence stacked up, defend, uphold, rescue, save, set against a single verb of failure in verse 2. Judges who were meant to act are accused of one long omission.

The psalm sits inside what scholars call the Elohistic Psalter, roughly Psalms 42 to 83, where the collectors prefer the general title Elohim to the personal name. That preference suits this poem unusually well, since the whole point is what it means to be called by that title. Psalm 82 is also the second of a pair with Psalm 81, where God says His people would not listen to Him, and Psalm 83 follows with a prayer against nations conspiring together. The book moves from a judgment inside the assembly to a threat from outside it.
context.historical:
Israel had an unusual habit in its law of using the word elohim for people who decide a case. In the rules about a servant who chooses to stay with his master, and in the rules about disputed property, the matter is brought "before the judges", Exodus 21:6 and Exodus 22:8-9, where the Hebrew behind "judges" is the very word translated "gods" in this psalm. The idea was that a court was a place where God's own verdict was being sought, and the person on the bench spoke for Him. Moses charged the judges he appointed to hear small and great alike and to show no partiality, "for judgment belongs to God," Deuteronomy 1:16-17. Centuries later King Jehoshaphat gave the same charge to the judges he placed in every fortified city of Judah: "you are not judging for man, but for the LORD," and with the LORD "there is no injustice or partiality or bribery," 2 Chronicles 19:5-7.

Against that background the charge in Psalm 82:2 is concrete. Cases were heard at the city gate, where elders sat, and a bribe, a favour to a wealthy family, or a silence about the widow's claim could tilt the outcome. The three groups God names in verses 3 and 4, the weak and fatherless, the afflicted and the needy, are the same groups the law protects again and again, for example Deuteronomy 10:17-18 and Deuteronomy 27:19. These people had no land, no household head, and no one to speak for them.

We do not know the psalm's precise date. It carries the name of Asaph, whose family led Israel's worship from David's time, 1 Chronicles 16:4-5. The Old Testament also knows of a heavenly gathering where the LORD sits with the host of heaven standing by Him, 1 Kings 22:19, Job 1:6 and Psalm 89:5-7. The ancient reader would therefore hear verse 1 against two backdrops at once, a human court and a heavenly one, and would not find it strange that the psalm keeps both in view. What the first hearers would not have missed is the shock: the powerful who sat in judgment were being sentenced by the One whose name they used.
context.canonical:
The psalm belongs to a large family of texts that hold power to account. Psalm 58 opens in a nearly parallel way: "Do you indeed speak justly, O rulers?" and goes on to say that in their hearts they devise injustice, Psalm 58:1-2. Psalm 72 is the positive counterpart, a prayer that the king will vindicate the afflicted and crush the oppressor, Psalm 72:1-4. The prophets take up the same complaint, Isaiah 1:17 and Jeremiah 22:15-16, where Jeremiah gives the striking line that taking up the cause of the poor and needy is what it means to know the LORD. That last text explains the odd phrase in Psalm 82:5, "They do not know or understand": in the Bible's own language, to know God is to do justice, and to fail at justice is to show that one does not know Him.

The psalm's language about "gods" is picked up in two directions. Ezekiel 28:2 and 28:9 turns it against the ruler of Tyre, who says "I am a god" and is told he will be only a man in the hands of those who wound him. That is the same lesson as Psalm 82:7. Isaiah 24:21 speaks of a day when the LORD punishes the host of heaven above and the kings of the earth below, a pairing that suits the two readings of the psalm's audience without forcing a choice.

In the New Testament, John 10:34-36 quotes verse 6 directly, in a conversation set at the Feast of Dedication, John 10:22. Paul speaks of principalities and powers in Ephesians 6:12 and Colossians 1:16, and of the saints one day judging the world and even angels, 1 Corinthians 6:2-3. The final line of the psalm, "Arise, O God, judge the earth," finds its answer in Acts 17:31, where God has fixed a day to judge the world with justice through a Man He appointed and has proved it by raising Him from the dead.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Asaph did not write this psalm to settle a question about the heavenly world for its own sake. He wrote it to be sung, in the presence of the people, so that every person who held authority over another would hear a verdict on that authority. The first hearers were meant to leave with a settled conviction that no title, however grand, exempts its holder from answering to the One who gave it. The psalm names one failure, favouring the wicked, and one duty, defending those who cannot defend themselves, and it makes the second the test of the first.

The author also wanted the powerless to hear something. A fatherless child or a widow in the gate could not answer a corrupt judge, but this psalm tells them that the bench itself has a Judge above it, that He notices, and that He is not indifferent. The last verse turns the whole scene into a prayer, which is a way of saying that when courts fail, the right response is neither cynicism nor violence but an appeal to the highest court of all. The closing claim that all the nations are God's inheritance lifts the horizon beyond Israel's own gates, so that even the rulers of other peoples are ultimately answerable to Him.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
What the psalm describes is a scene: a divine assembly, an indictment, a sentence. It does not describe a practice Israel was supposed to repeat, and it does not give a procedure for removing a corrupt official. The sentence of verse 7 is God's to carry out, not ours. Readers who take the psalm as licence to declare a particular leader an enemy of God, or to bring down an officeholder by their own hand, have moved from what the text records to something it never asks.

What the psalm prescribes is in the commands of verses 3 and 4, and these are direct. Defend, uphold, rescue and save are imperatives addressed to anyone who holds any kind of power, and in a modern setting that reaches beyond magistrates to employers, landlords, church leaders, teachers and parents. A person does not need a title to carry the duty; it belongs to whoever has the ability to speak or act for someone who cannot. The measure the psalm sets is what is done for the weak, not the sincerity of one's religion. James says something close when he calls care for orphans and widows in their distress pure and undefiled religion, James 1:27.

debates.question: Who are the 'gods' addressed in this psalm?

views.label: Human judges or rulers, exercising a God-given office of judgment
views.case: Israel's law uses the same word for those who decide a case, Exodus 21:6 and Exodus 22:8-9. The charges are court charges: partiality to the wicked, neglect of the weak. Verse 7 says they will die like mortals, which is a natural rebuke to men who thought themselves untouchable. Jesus reads the psalm this way in John 10:34-36, calling them those to whom the word of God came.

views.label: Members of the divine council, spiritual beings who ruled the nations under God
views.case: Verse 1 places the scene in an assembly of God, the setting of 1 Kings 22:19 and Psalm 89:5-7. Verse 5 speaks of the foundations of the earth shaking, which goes beyond a village court. Deuteronomy 32:8-9 in the BSB says the boundaries of the peoples were set 'according to the number of the sons of God', which some read as spiritual powers assigned to the nations. On this view verse 7 announces that they, too, will lose their standing and die.

views.label: A deliberately double address, both human rulers and the unseen powers behind them
views.case: Isaiah 24:21 puts 'the host of heaven above' and 'the kings of the earth below' under a single judgment, and Ephesians 6:12 speaks of struggle against rulers and authorities in heavenly places. The psalm never names its audience with precision, so the same charge can stand for every power that abuses delegated authority, seen or unseen.

debates.bearing: The two ends of the range agree on the main point: whoever holds authority holds it on loan, and the loan is called in. The choice affects how literally to take verse 7, but not the duty of verses 3 and 4. A reader who prefers the human reading should still notice why the psalm was placed in an assembly, and a reader who prefers the divine council reading should still hear the courtroom in verse 2.

debates.question: What does the sentence of verse 7 mean: 'like mortals you will die'?

views.label: The rulers will lose their office and their lives like anyone else
views.case: Ezekiel 28:9 shows the same pattern, where a ruler who calls himself a god is told he will be only a man in the hands of those who wound him. Death is the great leveller, and the psalm uses it to strip the pretension from human power.

views.label: The spiritual powers will lose the authority they misused
views.case: If the audience are unseen powers, dying like mortals is the reverse of their supposed status, a fall from the heights like the king pictured in Isaiah 14:12-15. The sentence then describes an overthrow more than a funeral, and it matches New Testament language about principalities being stripped of power.

debates.bearing: Either way, the sentence turns the title 'sons of the Most High' into a question about behaviour. Sonship without likeness to the Father has no protection, and the judgment falls on those who took the honour but refused the character. That fits how the New Testament speaks of the Son who both bears the title and lives up to it, Luke 1:32.

study.originalLanguages:
The most important word in the psalm is also the most common, elohim. It is a plural form, and it is used here in two different ways. When it describes the Judge in verse 1, it takes a singular verb, and translators write "God." When it describes those who stand before Him, it takes a plural sense and is written "gods." The same word carries the sense of a being who has real authority and power, and in Israel's usage that could be applied to the LORD without limit, to angelic beings, or, as in Exodus 21:6 and Exodus 22:8-9, to human judges. Nothing in the word itself settles who is meant, and the psalm exploits the ambiguity. What matters is the direction of derivation: the accused are elohim only because the LORD is Elohim.

The phrase "divine assembly" in verse 1 renders a Hebrew expression that literally reads "the assembly of El," where El is another ancient name for God. The verb "presides" is the Niphal participle of natsav, to take one's stand, and it is the posture of someone who has stepped up to open a proceeding. The verb that follows, shaphat, means to judge, but it carries a wider sense than pronouncing a verdict. It covers the whole work of setting a community right: ruling, restoring, delivering. This is why, in the book of Judges, the deliverers are called shophetim, and why verse 8 can ask God to "judge the earth" and mean that He should set it right. A reader who hears only "punish" misses half the word.

Verse 2 uses an idiom that does not survive translation. To "show partiality" the Hebrew says, literally, "to lift up faces," tis'u penei. A judge who lifts a face is one who looks at who is standing before him and gives weight to the wrong thing. Deuteronomy 10:17 uses the same idiom of God, who lifts no face, and the BSB footnote on the verse shows how it has sometimes been read as "defend the unjust." In verse 3 the verb translated "uphold the rights of" is a form of tsadaq, the root of righteousness, in a causative form: to declare righteous, to vindicate. Justice, in this sense, is something a court does for a person, not merely something it recognises in them.

Verse 5 gives the diagnosis, "They do not know or understand." The pair yada, to know, and bin, to discern, belongs to the language of wisdom. In Jeremiah 22:15-16, knowing the LORD is defined by taking up the cause of the poor. The judges' ignorance is therefore a moral ignorance and not a lack of information. The "foundations of the earth" that shake are the mosdei arets, the pillars that hold the ordered world in place, and Psalm 75:3 has God Himself saying that He bears up its pillars. The verb for shaking, mot, is the same one the psalmists use for the righteous who must not be moved, and here it warns that when justice fails, the ordered world starts to slide.

In verse 7 the BSB reads "like mortals," and the Hebrew is ke'adam, literally "like Adam" or "like man." The same word is the name of the first human, so that the phrase quietly recalls what happened in Genesis 3, where the one who had been given dominion returned to dust. The parallel line, "like rulers you will fall," uses the word for princes or chiefs. The verb "fall" is naphal, the same verb used of the fall of mighty men in many texts.

Finally, the last verse contains the verb nachal, to inherit, in the phrase "for all the nations are Your inheritance." The verb is imperfect, so it can equally be read "You will inherit all the nations." That reading fits Psalm 2:8, where the nations are promised to the Son as His inheritance. In the Septuagint, which John 10:34 follows in quoting verse 6, the word for "gods" is theoi, and the same Greek word is used when Jesus quotes the psalm. Nothing in that translation makes the accused any less accountable.

typology.type: The Judge who takes His stand, verse 1
typology.fulfillment: God stepping into the assembly to try those who abused their office points to the day when the Father's judgment is carried out by the Son. John says the Father has given all judgment to the Son, John 5:22, and grounds it in His being the Son of Man, John 5:27. Paul preaches the same to Athens: God has fixed a day to judge the world with justice through a Man He has appointed and has given proof by raising Him from the dead, Acts 17:31. The picture is not fully matched until the risen Christ sits as Judge; the psalm shows the courtroom without yet naming the Man on the bench.

typology.type: The defence of the weak, verses 3 and 4
typology.fulfillment: The commands the rulers refused to obey are the ones Jesus carries out. At Nazareth He reads that the Spirit has anointed Him to preach good news to the poor, to proclaim liberty to the captives and to release the oppressed, Luke 4:18. Matthew, quoting Isaiah, presents Him as the Servant who will not break a bruised reed and who will lead justice to victory, Matthew 12:18-20. Where the judges of the psalm favoured the powerful, Christ takes the side of those with no defender. The type falls short at one point: the psalm asks for defence of the weak, but Christ goes further and takes their place, bearing the penalty Himself, 1 Peter 2:24.

typology.type: The 'sons of the Most High' who die like Adam, verses 6 and 7
typology.fulfillment: The rulers are called sons of the Most High and then told they will die like Adam. The word of sonship is real, but it does not save them, because sonship without faithfulness is empty. Luke's Gospel announces that Mary's child will be called the Son of the Most High, Luke 1:32, and the genealogy ends by tracing His line to Adam, the son of God, Luke 3:38. Paul calls Adam a pattern of the One to come, Romans 5:14. Where the failed sons return to the dust, the true Son passes through death and rises. Believers are then brought in as children and co-heirs, Romans 8:14-17, as a gift and not as an achievement.

typology.type: The nations as God's inheritance, verse 8
typology.fulfillment: The psalm ends by handing the nations to God as His own. Psalm 2:8 spells out how: the Father gives the nations to the Son as His inheritance. Hebrews 1:2 describes the Son as the one God appointed heir of all things, and Revelation 11:15 announces that the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of the Lord and of His Christ. The correspondence is direct, and the escalation is that the inheritance is no longer only claimed in prayer but taken up in person. The type is unfinished in one respect: Revelation 21:24 shows the kings of the earth bringing their glory into the city, so the nations that were once judged are seen bringing honour to the Lamb's city.

study.christ:
The psalm leads to Christ first through the one New Testament text that quotes it, and that text is worth reading in its setting. In John 10:22-33 Jesus is walking in the temple courts at the Feast of Dedication when opponents demand that He say plainly whether He is the Christ. He answers by pointing to His works and to the unity between Himself and the Father, and they pick up stones. Then He turns to their own Scripture: "Is it not written in your Law: 'I have said you are gods'?" John 10:34. He goes on: "If he called them gods to whom the word of God came, and the Scripture cannot be broken, then what about the One whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world?" John 10:35-36. His argument moves from the lesser to the greater. If a passage of Scripture can address unjust human judges with the title "gods" because the word of God came to them, no one is entitled to call it blasphemy when the One whom the Father sanctified and sent says that He is God's Son. The point of the quotation is not that Jesus is one god among many. Elsewhere in the same conversation He says, "I and the Father are one," John 10:30. Rather, He shows that the opponents' own Bible leaves room for what He is claiming, while His works, John 10:37-38, are the real evidence.

There is a deeper irony. In Psalm 82 the rulers are condemned because they failed at the one thing a bearer of God's word must do, protect the helpless. Jesus, in the same chapter of John, speaks of Himself as the Good Shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep, John 10:11, and He declares that no one can snatch His sheep out of His hand, John 10:28. The unjust judges abandoned the vulnerable; the Shepherd stays with them at the cost of His life. In that sense the psalm, quoted almost in passing, throws Jesus' whole ministry into relief.

The psalm also leads to Christ through the closing prayer. "Arise, O God, judge the earth" is a cry for a judge who is impartial, who cannot be bribed, and who is not himself under judgment. The New Testament says that this Judge has been appointed, that He is a Man, and that His resurrection is the public proof, Acts 17:31. The Father has given all judgment to the Son, John 5:22. That means that the standard set for the rulers in verses 3 and 4 is the standard by which every life will be measured. Yet this is not only bad news. The One who will judge is the same One who took the place of the accused. Paul draws the contrast when he says there is now no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus, Romans 8:1, and that it is God who justifies, and Christ who intercedes, Romans 8:33-34.

Finally, verse 7 says that sons of the Most High will die like Adam. Christ is the Son of the Most High who does not fail. Luke 1:32 gives Him that title, and His victory over death shows the sentence of verse 7 has no hold on Him. Because He shares His sonship, believers are adopted and become co-heirs, Romans 8:17, and so the psalm's sentence on failed sons finds its reversal in the Son who succeeded. The reading should be held with care: the psalm does not predict Christ by name, and its charge is against actual rulers of its own day. The links come from the New Testament's own use of the passage and from its themes of judgment, sonship and inheritance.
study.god:
The first thing to notice about God in this psalm is where He stands. He is not asked to come to the assembly; He is already there and has already taken His stand, verse 1. The psalm assumes what much of the Bible affirms, that God is present at every seat of power, whether it is a village gate, a palace or a council chamber, and that no seat of power is out of His sight. This presence is not neutral. He has come to give judgment. The picture makes the doctrine of God's omnipresence personal: He is not merely everywhere, He is at the trial, listening to how the case was handled.

Second, the psalm reveals a God whose sovereignty is expressed as concern for the weak. The commands of verses 3 and 4 list the people He cares about: the fatherless, the afflicted, the oppressed, the needy. These are not incidental. Deuteronomy 10:17-18 says the LORD is God of gods and Lord of lords, showing no partiality and accepting no bribe, and in the same breath it says He executes justice for the fatherless and widow. His greatness and His gentleness belong together. The psalm does not let anyone picture God as a distant monarch who is indifferent to who gets treated well and who does not.

Third, God is the source of all derived authority. The word elohim is applied to human judges because they exercise something that belongs to Him. The doctrine implied is that all lawful authority, whether of magistrates, parents, kings or teachers, is a stewardship, and stewards give an account. Romans 13:1 says that there is no authority except from God, which is a comfort for the ruled and a warning to the ruling. In this psalm the warning is severe, since God pronounces sentence on those who abused it. The title is real, the trust is real, and so is the sentence.

Fourth, God's justice is both moral and ordered. The rulers are told in verse 5 that the foundations of the earth shake when they refuse to judge rightly. This implies that God has built a world in which justice is structural, not decorative; a society that lets the weak be crushed is not merely unkind, it is against the grain of creation. Psalm 75:3 sets this beside the claim that God Himself bears up the pillars of the earth. The upholder of the world and the Judge of the world are the same.

Fifth, the psalm shows God as the God of all nations. Verse 8 does not ask Him to judge Israel only. It asks Him to judge the earth, for all the nations are His inheritance. This universal reach is one of the boldest claims in the Psalter, since Israel was small and its courts were not among the great powers. The claim is not one of national pride but of accountability: God is not Israel's private possession, and His justice reaches to the rulers of Egypt, Babylon and Rome.

For worship, the psalm asks for a particular kind of honesty. We are meant to praise the God who judges, not simply the God who comforts, and to pray "Arise" when we see power abused. It also asks each of us to look at the small circles where we hold a little authority and to ask whether we are defending the weak or favouring the strong. The God of verse 1 is not a threat to those who love justice. He is the ally they have been waiting for.

crossReferences.note: In the law of disputed property, both parties bring their case before the judges, using the very Hebrew word that Psalm 82 translates 'gods.' The law already treated a court as a place where God's verdict is sought. That is why the psalm can rebuke judges as 'gods' without inventing a new idea: it holds them to the title Israel's own law had given.

Moses tells the judges to hear small and great alike and to show no partiality, 'for judgment belongs to God.' The reason given here is the ground of the whole psalm. If judgment belongs to God, a judge is only a borrower, and the borrower answers to the owner for how the trust was used.

The LORD is God of gods and Lord of lords, accepts no bribe, and executes justice for the fatherless and widow. The passage shows that supremacy and care for the vulnerable are not rival attributes in Israel's faith. Psalm 82 asks earthly judges to imitate the Judge who is over every other power.

Jehoshaphat places judges in every fortified city and tells them they judge for the LORD, with whom there is no injustice, partiality or bribery. It is a real historical moment when the ideal of Psalm 82 was put into practice, and it shows what the psalm would have sounded like to a king who had just made such appointments.

Another Psalm of the same tension: 'Do you indeed speak justly, O rulers?' The answer is that in their hearts they devise injustice. Psalm 58 continues with the plea for God to break their teeth, while Psalm 82 goes straight to a verdict. Read together, they give both the accusation and the sentence against corrupt rule.

The prophet says that King Josiah took up the cause of the poor and needy and adds, 'Is this not what it means to know Me?' This explains the diagnosis of Psalm 82:5. To 'know' God is not only to hold correct ideas about Him but to share His concern, so a judge who neglects the poor shows he does not know the One whose office he holds.

The prince of Tyre says, 'I am a god,' and is told, 'you are a man and not a god.' The passage is a clear case of the lesson in Psalm 82:7: human power that thinks itself divine will be exposed as mortal. It also shows that the biblical writers were not shy about using the word 'god' as a charge against arrogant rulers.

The Father says to the anointed King, 'I will make the nations Your inheritance.' This is the promise that stands behind the final line of Psalm 82. Where the psalm asks God to judge the earth because the nations are already His, Psalm 2 shows how they will be given: through the Son who asks.

Jesus cites verse 6 to answer a charge of blasphemy. He reasons that if Scripture uses 'gods' of those to whom the word of God came, then the Son whom the Father sanctified and sent cannot be blamed for saying He is God's Son. The quotation is a hinge in John's Gospel, and it shows how carefully Jesus read the Psalms.

Paul says the saints will judge the world and even angels. That is a surprising echo of the psalm, in which those who once judged are themselves judged. In Christ, the position of those who share His rule is not a matter of title but of union with the true Judge, and the judgment of the world is put into the hands of a people who were once on trial themselves.

God has fixed a day to judge the world with justice through a Man He appointed, and He has given proof by raising Him from the dead. The prayer of Psalm 82:8 is answered here. The Judge is identified, His authority is proved, and His justice is announced to the nations.

On that day the LORD punishes the host of heaven above and the kings of the earth below. The verse joins the two possible audiences of Psalm 82 in one judgment, and it lets a reader hold both readings of the word 'gods' without forcing a choice between the heavenly and the earthly.

study.oneStory:
The psalm answers a question left open since the early chapters of Genesis. Human beings were made in God's image and given dominion, Genesis 1:26-28, so that authority was meant to be an expression of His character. Genesis 3 shows that authority can be turned into self-serving power, and Genesis 4 shows its first fruit in a brother's blood. From then on the Bible keeps returning to the same question: who will govern the world as God would, and what happens to those who do not? Psalm 82 asks that question of the ordinary courts and the unseen powers alike, and the sentence is the same as it was at the beginning: return to the dust.

The story moves along the line of the deliverers. Israel is led out of Egypt by a man God made "like God to Pharaoh," Exodus 7:1, and who then hands the work of judging to appointed judges, Exodus 18:21-22. The book of Judges shows the office decaying, and the books of Kings show that the monarchy fails in the same way. The prophets accuse the rulers of devouring the vineyard and crushing the poor, Isaiah 3:14-15. Each of these failures deepens the ache that Psalm 82:8 puts into words. The story needs a judge who does not fail.

That Judge is Jesus. He is the Son of the Most High, Luke 1:32, whom the Father has appointed to judge the world, Acts 17:31 and John 5:22. In His ministry He does what the rulers of the psalm would not, defending the poor and releasing the oppressed, Luke 4:18. On the cross He goes further and takes the sentence on Himself, so that those condemned as sons who die like Adam may be brought in as children and co-heirs, Romans 8:14-17. The church is then given a share in His work: Paul speaks of the saints judging the world, 1 Corinthians 6:2-3, and the call to defend the fatherless and widow becomes part of what it means to belong to Him, James 1:27.

The new creation is where the psalm's prayer is answered. Revelation 11:15 announces that the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ. The rulers who abused their power are gone, and the King of kings, Revelation 19:16, rules with justice. The nations are no longer a battleground of competing powers but the inheritance of the Son, and the kings of the earth bring their glory into the city, Revelation 21:24. The last verse of the psalm is not left as a hope only. It becomes a description of the world made right.

sermon.title: Putting the Gods in Their Place
sermon.why: Piper works through Psalm 82 verse by verse, explaining the 'gods' as delegated powers standing under God's judgment and showing how the psalm's closing plea, 'arise, O God, judge the earth,' anchors hope in God's ultimate ownership and justice over all nations.

quiz.q: Where does God take His stand in this psalm, verse 1?

options.text: In the divine assembly, rendering judgment among the gods.
options.note: Verse 1 sets this exact courtroom scene.

options.text: In a private meeting with only the king.
options.note: The scene is a public, assembly-wide judgment, not a private royal audience.

options.text: Nowhere; the psalm describes no such scene.
options.note: Verse 1 explicitly describes God presiding in judgment.

options.text: In a foreign nation's temple.
options.note: The setting is the divine assembly over the 'gods,' not a foreign temple.

quiz.q: What charge does God bring against the 'gods,' verses 2-4?

options.text: Judging unjustly and showing partiality to the wicked instead of defending the weak, fatherless, afflicted, and oppressed.
options.note: This is the exact charge laid out in verses 2-4.

options.text: Failing to build enough temples.
options.note: The charge concerns justice for the vulnerable, not temple construction.

options.text: Collecting too many taxes from the wealthy.
options.note: The concern is partiality toward the wicked and neglect of the weak, not taxation policy.

options.text: Refusing to go to war.
options.note: The charge is about unjust judgment, not military decisions.

quiz.q: What is the effect of the 'gods' moral blindness, verse 5?

options.text: All the foundations of the earth are shaken.
options.note: Verse 5 states this consequence directly.

options.text: The nation becomes wealthier and more stable.
options.note: The described effect is instability and shaking, not prosperity.

options.text: Nothing changes at all.
options.note: The text describes a real, destabilizing effect, not the absence of consequence.

options.text: Only the judges themselves are affected.
options.note: The effect described is cosmic and societal, 'foundations of the earth,' not limited to the judges alone.

quiz.q: What verdict does God pronounce on the 'gods' despite their exalted title, verses 6-7?

options.text: Though called 'sons of the Most High,' they will die like mortals and fall like any ruler.
options.note: Verses 6-7 pronounce exactly this verdict of mortality.

options.text: They will be granted eternal life regardless of their conduct.
options.note: The verdict is mortality and fall, the opposite of unconditional eternal reward.

options.text: They will be promoted to even higher office.
options.note: The verdict is a humbling fall, not a promotion.

options.text: They will be forgiven without any consequence.
options.note: The text pronounces a real verdict of mortality, not an absence of consequence.

quiz.q: How does Jesus use this psalm in John 10:34-36?

options.text: He cites verse 6 to argue that if Scripture calls human authorities 'gods,' His own claim to be the Son of God is not blasphemy.
options.note: This is exactly how Jesus reasons from this psalm in John 10.

options.text: He uses it to deny that He is divine.
options.note: Jesus uses the psalm to defend, not deny, His divine sonship.

options.text: He uses it to argue that all people are gods in the same sense He is.
options.note: Jesus' argument distinguishes His unique sonship from the psalm's human judges, not equates them.

options.text: He quotes it to predict the fall of the Roman Empire.
options.note: Jesus applies the verse to His own identity, not to Roman political history.

questions: Every human authority in this psalm holds power only by God's delegation, verse 6-7. Where do you exercise authority, whether at home, work, or elsewhere, and how does knowing it is borrowed change how you use it?

God's charge against the judges is specific: defend the weak, fatherless, afflicted, and oppressed, verses 3-4. Who in your own circle of influence is weak or overlooked, and what would it look like to actively defend their cause?
The psalm says corrupted leadership makes 'the foundations of the earth' shake, verse 5. Where do you see the effects of injustice destabilizing trust and stability around you today?
Even those called 'gods' will 'die like mortals,' verse 7. How does remembering your own mortality shape the way you use whatever authority or influence you have been given?
The psalm ends with a prayer, 'arise, O God, judge the earth,' verse 8. What situation of injustice are you tempted to fix yourself rather than bringing honestly to God in prayer?

translationNotes.note: 'Gods' (elohim) here refers to human judges or rulers exercising delegated authority, as in Exodus 22:28, not to rival deities; the same Hebrew word is simply God's ordinary name elsewhere in the Psalter.
'How long will you judge unjustly' can also be rendered 'how long will you defend the unjust,' with the same basic charge of corrupted judgment either way.
'Sons of the Most High' identifies the judges' derived, God-given office and authority, the very phrase Jesus draws on in John 10:34-36 to defend His own unique divine sonship.
